newsitem.title: FINLAND: FEATURE-Unhealthy eating poses epidemic threat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Unhealthy eating poses epidemic threat.

text.p: It can start with symptoms so vague you may not notice them, but it can kill. Now experts say diabetes is growing so fast that an epidemic is on the way.
Already the fourth main cause of death in many countries, diabetes affects 135 million people worldwide and experts say the number of sufferers is rising sharply.

"By 2010 there will be 240 million diabetics, the majority of them in developing countries," said Professor Marja-Riita Taskinen of the University of Helsinki, who will head a major international conference on the disease here this week.
She was citing research by Australian Professor Paul Zimmet into non-insulin-dependent or "type two" diabetes, which affects 90 percent of sufferers and mainly hits adults.

"That means we will have a diabetes epidemic in the world," Taskinen said. Around 8,000 scientists and diabetes specialists will focus on that prospect at the conference, including drugs firms eager to promote new discoveries in treatment.

Driving the increase in diabetes are the world's ageing population, and modern lifestyles where people eat too much of the wrong kind of foods, become overweight and do not take enough exercise, says conference organiser, the International Diabetes Federation.
Statistically, that clearly spells America. In the United States and Canada, diabetes is the third largest cause of death by disease, above breast cancer and lung cancer.

But the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, as well as Southeast Asia and especially India, are also showing sharp increases. And the federation sees major risks as China's population becomes Westernised.
NO CURE - BUT INJECTIONS FOR SOME

There is no cure for diabetes -- and people who suffer from the insulin-dependent or "type one" strain, which most commonly starts in children and adolescents -- must inject themselves with insulin up to four times a day to stay alive.

Scientists have found no other method of treatment in the 75 years since Canadian Leonard Thomas received the first injection, said Mary-Francis McKenna, 24-year-old editor of the Irish Diabetic Association's magazine.
She has had diabetes since she was 10.
"Why should I still be taking insulin injections?" she said. "It's extraordinary. To think that 75 years have gone by."
The problem may be that, while diabetes can kill, in itself it rarely does. More often it is the killer complications associated with the condition -- especially heart disease -- that claim lives.
The exact cause of diabetes is not known, but it starts with the body failing to produce insulin (type one) or failing to produce insulin effectively (type two).
Insulin regulates the level of sugar in the blood, so without it blood-sugar levels skyrocket.
McKenna described the warning signals for type two: "Number one is you are overweight. Number two is if you're drinking slightly more and going to the toilet more than feels normal.
"Are you getting out of bed at night to go to the toilet on a regular basis?
"Then there's general tiredness and irritability, and if there's a history of diabetes in your family you should surely get tested."
The drinking and urinating comes from the fact that the body is trying to flush out the extra sugar, she explained.
Why heavier people are more prone is not entirely clear, but statistically the risk is higher in overweight people who exercise less than others.
People who are aged over 40 or pregnant with a large baby are also more at risk, according to the federation.
TAKING RISKS TO AVOID COMA
"The problem with diabetes is that long-term complications are caused by high blood-sugar levels," said McKenna. "That damages smaller blood vessels."
That in turn restricts the blood supply to eyes, kidneys, feet -- causing blindness, kidney failure, or forcing amputation.
Although McKenna has got used to the lifestyle the disease imposes, the way she talks illustrates how tough it can be for sufferers to manage life.

Healthy eating is not just an option. Checking your insulin level by pricking your finger before meals is routine. Remember to pop into the bathroom to inject insulin before you start your lunch with friends.

Then there is the risk of letting your blood sugar fall too low and passing out, perhaps in public. Some sufferers try to avoid that by keeping their blood sugar slightly higher than it should be, but McKenna says they risk serious longer-term damage.

"It's a big pain for people who are susceptible to 'going low'," she said. "They are constantly going to keep blood sugar levels higher than they should to avoid the embarrassment of going into a coma."
NO GLAMOUR IN 'SAFE FOOD'?
For those concerned that they are at risk, the good news is that, for the most common form of diabetes, type two, pills are usually enough to supplement the discipline of diet and exercise.
But Taskinen points out that the cost of medication, not to mention treatment for all the complications, risks being a major headache for governments and all those involved.
"If we want to do something it means prevention," she said. "The treatment of obesity is very difficult. We need more education."
Teaching people to eat well -- assuming they can afford to -- is a tough responsibility for governments competing with commerce and all the attractions of a 'more modern' lifestyle.

And a key point for both McKenna and Taskinen is that, even though diabetes directly affects many more people worldwide than AIDS, it does not attract the dramatic publicity generated by the gradual collapse of the human immune system.
"The difference of course is that AIDS is killing faster," said Taskinen. "Diabetes has been known for many years. Progress is slower."

So McKenna, a confident and articulate professional who cheerfully accepts that she does not have the world's most "poignant, heart-rending condition", is still waiting for a day when she does not wake up thinking of a needle.
